back: Segmentation (identify segments) → Targeting (select segments) → Positioning (create competitive advantage). Better meets needs → loyalty → higher share and profitability, fewer resources needed over time.
Traditional demographics lose predictive power; people construct lifestyles and identities of their own choosing.
Identifying and grouping consumers into relatively homogeneous segments based on shared needs, characteristics, attitudes or behaviours, to target them with tailored strategies.

I Planning & design (objectives, resources) · II Qualitative assessment (database review, deep needs) · III Quantitative measurement (sample, questionnaire, data) · IV Analysis & implementation (cluster analysis, profiling, database tools).
Bases: variables that form segments (why they differ – needs, attitudes, behaviour). Descriptors: profile and reach segments (demographics, firmographics, values, purchase frequency).
Groups consumers on several variables: minimise distance within clusters, maximise distance between centroids. Robustness: split sample randomly in two, re-run, compare agreement.
I Size & growth · II Structural characteristics (competition, saturation, protectability, environmental risk) · III Product-market fit (fit, relationship with other segments, profitability).
Single segment · selective specialisation · range of offerings to one segment · many offerings to many segments · full market coverage.
Specify & weight drivers → rate segments → weights × ratings → plot (attractiveness × company strengths) → sensitivity analysis.

Strong: protect/refocus (low) · expand selectively (avg) · build preemptive position (high).
Medium: strict cash flow (low) · preserve position (avg) · expand selectively (high).
Weak: exit (low) · harvest (avg) · capitalize on attractiveness (high).
Differentiation: tangible/intangible differences vs competitors. Positioning: strategies to differentiate the offering in the minds of target customers – distinct, relevant, sustainable.
Target segment → competitive offerings → differentiator dimensions → customer ratings → perceptual map → integrate preferences/choice/share → positioning statement.
Visual image of consumers' mental landscape: short distance = similar brands; axes = underlying dimensions; vectors = attributes. Easy to read, but oversimplifies.
Network of associations around a brand (e.g. Nielsen, from consumer conversations); proximity = statistical correlation; no fixed axes; rich but subjective.

Least satisfied → lowest satisfaction score. Focus → highest importance scores of that cluster. Attractiveness → size, satisfaction, visit frequency. GE matrix needs company strengths – otherwise "not enough information".
